en: Until Almambet’s lion
Had taken wounds in eighty places.
“He meant to break my proud brow,
Carry off my people as plunder,
And would have broken my back.”
So spoke hero Seytek,
Telling it all to his lionhearted father,
Relating horrors no man could imagine.
His son Seytek told him this,
Speaking truth, not falsehood:
“When that mad brute thrust his spear,
No champion could stand against him.
I would have perished, had not
My forefather Manas upheld me.
My mind is weary and my strength is gone;
The savage swine has truly prevailed.”
When his son had spoken thus,
His father flared in anger, caring nothing,
Scorning the infidel, huge as Mount Karaskar,
As though he were not worth the hem of his robe.
The gray-maned chief of sixty champions
Rose in wrath and struck terror,
And had Buurul, his campaign steed,
Saddled once again from the beginning,
To face the warrior son of the monstrous giant,
And test him in combat;
To die if hostile fate had come,
Or grapple with him and strike with his spear,
And, if his surging strength prevailed,
To spill Sarybay’s blood.
His fury boiled and he ground stones in his teeth,
Eager to unleash a fearsome slaughter,
And wrest the Kyrgyz, blessed by Kyzır,
From the hands
Of the Kalmyks.
Seytek had grieved in deep distress.
O father, splendid champion, noble lion,
Clad in blue steel,
And made ready at the word “enemy”;
To the noble lion himself
Inspiration came from the unseen,
And power streamed from his majesty,
While Seytek’s wits had fled in panic.
From his father, the gray-maned warrior,
Seytek had fled that day.
He had raised many a battle cry,
Then gone to his gray-maned warrior father
And made his plea.
At the many-hued golden pavilion,
He said to hero Semetey:
“You became a champion, you became a lion;
I am Seytek, your son.
Unable to prevail against the foe I faced,
I was laid level with the black earth.
My strength and power failed;
The monstrous giant’s warrior son appeared,
And your son Seytek, your poor wretch,
Could not withstand the foe he challenged,
But was brought level with the black earth.
God did not take this helpless man;
Yet rather than leave a man alive—
The powerless have no honor,
And a shot fired into the world brings shame.
I burned and seethed like an ember;
Though born of a hero, I, Seytek,
Was as nothing beside Sarybay.
When we came face-to-face,
My whole body quivered,
My tiny soul cried out,
My noble head ran with blood,
And my entire frame was crushed.
My strong waist bent beneath me,
My strength ebbed and my gear hung loose,
And both my eyes bulged.
My arms failed, and I grieved;
I despaired of my beloved people.
He made my nation wail,
And utterly broke my back;
It was as though he tore out my very marrow,
As though he broke my spirit.
He bound and blighted my flourishing fortune,
This raging son of the monstrous giant.
To consume every foe he faced,
To sacrifice himself for his people,
To die if death had come,
And settle the account in earnest
With the savage, treacherous swine,
He rode out alone from the Kyrgyz,
His silhouette looming like a mountain.
He threw his dreadful enemy into confusion,
Making his peerless racer
Stride with a stately gait.
He brought it toward the tumult of the host;
Upon the steed huge as Ala-Too,
His father, the noble falcon and lion,
Rode at a rolling gallop.
Buurul sensed the enemy,
And raised his antler-like head.
He turned toward the direction
From which the mighty infidel would come,
Lengthening his stride like a wild ram.
The superb battle charger
Glared with eyes like a mountain ram’s,
Pinned back his ears like a wild ass,
And, truly destined for the unseen,
Swept the earth like a whirlwind.
No livestock could match
The pace of Buurul beneath him,
Nor could the wind match his gallop.
He drew tight the long reins,
And his hooves furrowed the earth,
As he raised his steel spear
And headed straight toward Sarybay.
From Sary’s curving ridge,
From the edge of Kötörmö,
He covered his awesome form
In armor no bullet could pierce;
Grieving in bitter wrath,
He fastened its nine clasps
And donned his battle coat.
He threw all before him into panic;
Behold the towering, mountain-like figure,
And the manifest prince’s
Fearsome aspect—
The hair on one’s socks would stand on end.
His eyes blazed like a hungry lion’s,
And he ground his teeth as he charged,
Roused like a starving lion;
The lionhearted hero’s majesty was unmatched,
And he roared in fury:
“Through all my years I have seen lions,
And I have seen hosts of warriors,
Yet it seems I had never truly seen one;
Alas, Sarybay, wretched soul,
It seems I have lived without dying.”
The bloodthirsty lion flew into a rage,
And readied all his weapons;
Crackling like lightning,
He prepared himself against Sarybay.
Sarybay was the one he would face,
He who had brought misery upon his descendants;
Such was the mighty clash.
The warrior’s keen edge
Was like well-tempered steel;
When a day of desperate battle dawns,
All true heroes are thus.
From Kanykey’s fortress,
From Aichürök’s encampment,
From the plains of Great Talas,
From the banks of Jylgyndy,
He stirred all the people into alarm,
Making the matchless charger
Stride with a proud, rolling gait.
Taking the wise and accomplished lion,
And the warrior companion as his support,
He went to wage single combat,
To drive the monstrous infidel’s son
All the way back to his own land,
To unleash a fearsome slaughter.
The hero girded himself in wrath
To deliver the Kyrgyz people
From calamity.
A gray tiger was his guardian;
No such soul existed in the world.
From Akyz, where no horse had trodden,
Suddenly, across the branching passes,
A sight appeared that divided the mind:
Sarybay, the monstrous giant’s son,
Loamed like a blue craggy mountain.
He carried a spear like a pine tree,
And his cast-iron mace, huge as Mount Opol,
Was strapped close at his side.
His shout split heads,
And his roar split stones.
Then Sarybay
Was seized by his blood-drinking fury,
And spared nothing before him.
He seemed able to leap across a ridge
And devour all humankind;
He loomed like a mountain where herds graze,
And the mad brute seemed ready
To seize and swallow anyone he met.
His form was strange and his venom strong—
Abandon all hope of your precious life.
They stood facing one another;
Sarybay and Semetey
Met and thrust their spears,
And began a mighty exchange of blows.
The watching people renounced
Their tiny lives entirely.
Spears bent when they charged;
“How can the two heroes survive?” they said,
Despairing of their mortal lives.
Sarybay, the monstrous giant’s son,
Was that accursed incendiary himself,
The very dark eye of the angel of death;
He devoured all he encountered,
And swallowed those who came near.
Of every creature that crossed his path,
Not one remained alive.
He froze those he charged upon,
And if his claws seized them,
He made them march at a ponderous pace.
Having heard the child’s report,
Having heard that the monstrous giant’s son
Was a brutal tyrant,
Having heard all the rumors,
And heard that no strength could prevail
Against the monstrous infidel’s son,
He showed himself a true lion.
Leaving all others behind,
His long life now drawing late,
He went to meet death at Sarybay’s hands,
To prove he would never retreat,
And test himself against Sarybay.
If his dear eyes closed in death,
He would leave his children and people
Thereafter to the savage enemy,
That vicious swine;
Still, he would test his strength and lion-heart
Against Sarybay.
He had grieved in life
And rejoiced when told he would die;
Born of an illustrious man,
Wherever he turned his face,
He carried tumult in his wake.
Descendant of a gray-maned lion,
He tore armored coats into four,
And his counterstroke was crimson fire.
He laid low all who opposed him;
None who grappled with him survived.
Whoever provoked his anger,
He drove before him,
And crushed between his fangs.
When the enemy met him, whole nations died;
Many giants perished grappling with him.
Your true gray-maned lion, your warrior prince,
Raised his steel spear,
And headed straight toward Sarybay,
A naked sword strapped at his side;
As though hail would pour down again,
Wrath spread across his face.
He seemed ready to trample down whoever faced him,
His fangs jutting fiercely,
The front of his saddle sagging beneath him.
His majesty appeared supreme,
And any man who watched him
Was left utterly bewildered.
His courage burned like fire
As he advanced upon the bloodthirsty lion,
Staring about like a devourer,
With all his weapons ready.
Relentless, he transformed in fury,
Raging in savage wrath,
And addressed the bloodthirsty lion:
“Sarybay, son of the monstrous giant,
